title: Jatayu's fight
hookLine: an old vulture flies up at the most feared king in the world
carry: life may go, the word must not
last: SAKSHI: THE WORLD IS OUR WITNESS.

cards: He's old, and Valmiki is clear about it. Jatayu, king of the vultures, has lived a long time, and he was a friend of Rama's father, Dasharatha.

When the brothers first came to Panchavati, he offered to watch over Sita whenever they were away. Now he wakes in his tree to her voice and sees a chariot overhead, with the most feared king in the world at the reins.
He doesn't do the math. He flies up.

teach.h: I'M OLD; YOU WON'T TAKE HER.
teach.b: He talks before he fights, one king to another. I'm old, he tells Ravana, and you're young, armed, in a chariot, with a bow. Still, you won't carry her off while I'm alive.
A king should protect other people's wives, not steal them. Put her down. Ravana doesn't.
So the old bird fights, and Valmiki gives him a real fight. Jatayu tears at Ravana with beak and talons.

He breaks his bow, smashes the chariot, kills the beasts that pull it, and knocks the driver from his seat. Then Ravana draws his sword and cuts off Jatayu's wings. The old king falls, and Ravana carries Sita on.
Remember what Jatayu said first: I'm old, you're young and armed.
He knew he'd lose. He fought because he'd said he would keep watch.

teach.h: PRAN JAYE PAR VACHAN NA JAYE.
teach.b: Hindu families still quote a line from Tulsidas, spoken by Rama's father, Dasharatha, Jatayu's old friend: Raghukul reet sada chali aayi, pran jaye par vachan na jaye.
The way of Raghu's line, Rama's family, has always been: life may go, but the word must not. Dasharatha kept his word to Kaikeyi, and it cost him his son. His old friend keeps his word in the sky.
In Hindu teaching a word given is part of dharma, part of satya, truth.
Now the week. A golden deer, and maya's shine. Maricha's last breath, and the name.
Lakshmana's bow. Many Ramayanas, one Rama. A robe that didn't make a sannyasi.

teach.h: LIFE MAY GO, THE WORD MUST NOT.
teach.b: And today, wings given for a word.

how: Jatayu is honored across India as a model of loyalty; places in Kerala, Andhra Pradesh and elsewhere hold local traditions about where he fell. Hindu families still quote Tulsidas's 'pran jaye par vachan na jaye' about keeping one's word.

games.q: tomorrow Rama finds Jatayu. from today's teaching, why do Hindus honor an old bird as a hero?
o: he kept his word to watch over Sita and gave his wings for dharma.
he won the fight against Ravana.
he was a god in disguise all along.
games.why: Jatayu lost the fight and kept his word. in Hindu teaching, a word given is part of dharma, and he paid for it with his wings.

practice: Before a puja or a fast, many Hindus make a sankalpa, a formal intention: a little water in the right palm, the promise said aloud, then the water let go.

Try it with one promise you've already made; small is fine, like a call you said you'd make. Hold a little water in your palm, or just cup your empty hand, say it, and let it go. If you don't pray, just say it out loud.

wordCard.voice: Jatayu. The old vulture king, friend of Dasharatha, who fights Ravana in the sky to keep his word, and falls.

orig.note: Sanskrit jaṭāyu, the vulture king. Valmiki also calls him gṛdhrarāja, king of vultures.

carryVoice: Your line: life may go, the word must not. Tomorrow, Rama finds the old bird. Another week, done.
